name: Hello Anchor
description: Hello world program with Anchor framework.

intro.promise: You'll write a small Solana program, put it live on devnet and call it with your name.

steps.title: Program
steps.objective: Define the hello instruction and log a message
steps.learned: Declaring a program and its instructions

beats.text: Every Anchor program opens with the same two lines: the import and the program's id. They're routine, so I've written them.

A program does its work in instructions: functions inside a module marked `#[program]`. Yours is `hello`. I'll put the module under those two lines, and you pick its one line of code. A program on Solana has no terminal: the only place it can write is the program log, which comes back with every transaction.

beats.question: Which line writes to the program log?
beats.right: Yes. `msg!` writes to the program log. I've put `hello` in the `#[program]` module, under the two lines.
why: `println!` prints to a terminal, and a program on Solana has none. On chain, a program talks through `msg!`.
That's TypeScript, and you'll use it in the client in step 3. Inside a Rust program the log line comes from `msg!`.
beats.hint: Think about where each line would print. A program on Solana runs on a validator, with no terminal and no console.
beats.typed: That's the line. `msg!` writes to the program log. I've put `hello` and the `#[program]` module around it.

beats.say: That's a whole program. Let's compile it.
beats.title: Build lib.rs
beats.context: Compiles lib.rs on Playground's build server

steps.failsWith: cannot find type `Hello` in this scope
steps.planned: This one's on purpose. Every Anchor developer meets this error once, so let's meet it now.

onFail.text: Line 9 asks for `Context<Hello>`: the accounts `hello` works with, described by a type called `Hello`. That type doesn't exist yet, so the compiler stops. `hello` reads no accounts, so the type can be empty. The fix goes at the bottom of lib.rs.

onFail.question: So what does `Context<Hello>` need?
onFail.right: Exactly. `#[derive(Accounts)]` tells Anchor which accounts an instruction expects. I've added an empty one at the bottom.
why: `Hello` does describe accounts, but it's a type in your code. The compiler needs it before anything reaches devnet.
`Hello` isn't part of Anchor. It's yours to declare: the list of accounts `hello` reads.
onFail.hint: The compiler wants a type in your own code that lists accounts.
onFail.typed: That's the line that fixes it: `#[derive(Accounts)]` tells Anchor the struct under it lists accounts. I've put the empty `Hello` under it.

onFail.say: Build again. This time it should pass.
onFail.title: Build lib.rs
onFail.context: Same build, now with the `Hello` struct

win.headline: Your program compiles
win.line: The build also made its IDL: one instruction, `hello`. That's what clients will call.

steps.explain: This step writes the smallest Anchor program there is: one instruction, `hello`, that writes a line to the program log. I explain a piece, you pick the right line, and I write it in. Then the build checks it.

steps.title: Build & Deploy

beats.text: Right now your program is only a build: Playground compiled it, but nobody can call it yet. Deploying uploads it to devnet, Solana's public test network, where anyone can call it. It costs devnet SOL, test money with no value. You get it from the devnet faucet with one button before the deploy, and if the faucet is busy, at faucet.solana.com. Before you press Deploy, a guess.

beats.question: What does a deploy give your program, so clients can find it?
options: A copy of lib.rs on devnet
beats.right: Yes. Every program lives at an address, its program id. Watch for it when the deploy lands.
why: A program isn't a web server, so there's no URL. Clients find it by its address and send it transactions.
Devnet keeps the compiled program, not your source. What clients need from it is its address.
beats.hint: Clients don't browse to a program. They send transactions to it. To what?
beats.skipped: No problem. A deploy gives your program an address, its program id. Watch for it.

beats.say: A deploy pays in devnet SOL. Get some for your wallet first.
beats.title: Get devnet SOL
beats.context: From the devnet faucet · free test SOL

beats.say: Press Deploy and watch for the program id.
beats.title: Deploy to devnet
beats.context: From your Playground wallet · free devnet SOL

win.headline: Your program is live on devnet
win.line: Its IDL also gave you the Call panel: a form for every instruction. You'll use it in a moment.

steps.explain: Deploying puts your built program on devnet, Solana's public test network, at an address of its own: the program id. It's paid from your Playground wallet in free devnet SOL. Press Deploy and wait for the id.

steps.title: Client
steps.objective: Call the instruction from the TypeScript client

beats.text: A client is code outside your program that sends it transactions, like the app your users will open. I've made `client/client.ts` for it.

In Playground, `pg.program` already knows your program from its IDL: `pg.program.methods` has one method per instruction. Calling one only builds the call; something still has to send it. Your line goes at the top of client.ts.

beats.question: Which line sends `hello` to devnet?
beats.right: Right. `.methods.hello()` builds the call and `.rpc()` sends it, then hands back the transaction's signature. I've added a line that prints it.
why: Close. Instructions live under `.methods`, not on `pg.program` itself.
That builds the call but never sends it. `.rpc()` does the sending.
beats.hint: Instructions live under `.methods`, and something has to send the call.
beats.typed: That's the line. `.methods.hello()` builds the call and `.rpc()` sends it. I've added the comment above it and a line under it that prints the signature.

beats.say: Run it and watch what comes back.
beats.title: Run client.ts
beats.context: Sends one transaction to devnet · fee from your wallet

win.headline: Your program answered from devnet
win.line: That `Hello, World!` is the `msg!` line from lib.rs, coming back in the transaction's logs. The Call panel makes the same call without code.
win.callPanelLine: You called `hello` from the Call panel, which Playground built from the IDL. In code, the same call is one line.

steps.explain: A client is code outside the program that sends it transactions. Here it's one line of TypeScript in `client.ts`. You can also call `hello` from the Call panel, no code needed.

steps.title: Name argument
steps.objective: Give hello a name argument and log it

beats.text: `hello` greets everyone the same way. Let's make it greet you. Anchor hands every instruction its `Context` first; anything the caller sends, like a name, is a plain argument. I'll change `hello`'s first line, line 9.

beats.question: Where does `name` go?
beats.right: Yes. The `Context` comes first, then your own arguments. I've also put `name` in the log line: `msg!` fills `{}` with it.
why: `Hello` lists the accounts `hello` reads, not values the caller sends. A name is plain data, so it's an argument.
Close, but Anchor expects the `Context` first. Your own arguments follow it.
beats.hint: A name is plain data the caller sends, not an account. Then think about the order Anchor expects.

writes.block:
pub fn hello(_ctx: Context<Hello>, name: String) -> Result<()> {
        msg!("Hello, {}!", name);

beats.key: fn hello(_ctx: Context<Hello>, name: String) -> Result<()> {
beats.typed: That's it: the `Context` first, then your own arguments. I've put `name` in the log line too: `msg!` fills `{}` with it.

beats.text: `hello` wants a name now, so the client has to send one. I've changed the call in `client/client.ts` to `hello("Anchor")`. Any name works; "Anchor" stands in for yours.

win.headline: hello knows your name
win.line: You changed an instruction, shipped the new version and called it with an argument.

steps.explain: Instructions can take arguments after their `Context`. This step adds a `name` to `hello`, ships the new version and calls it with your name.

finish.headline: You built and called your first Solana program
finish.line: Your greeting came back from devnet in a transaction your wallet signed.

chips.label: What should I build next?
chips.answer: Lumberjack is a good next one: it keeps a player's wood and energy in an account on chain and changes them, so you meet accounts for real.

chips.label: What is devnet SOL?
chips.answer: Devnet is Solana's public test network. Its SOL is free and worth nothing, so you can deploy and call as much as you like. You get it from the devnet faucet with one button; if the faucet is busy, get some yourself at faucet.solana.com.
